newsitem.title: USA: Westinghouse media unchained at last.
newsitem.headline: Westinghouse media unchained at last.

text.p: Westinghouse Electric Corp unveiled its plan to offer investors the pure media play they've craved since it acquired CBS Inc nearly a year ago.

Ending months of speculation, Westinghouse on Wednesday said it would split itself in two, spinning off Westinghouse Electric Co (WELCO) from the media company that will include CBS and radio syndicator Infinity Broadcasting.
While Westinghouse's broadcast business still will be shackled to the roughly $6 billion in debt owed by the parent, the escape from the plodding industrial segment drew acclaim.

"You're going to end up with an unencumbered opportunity for a direct play at the media company," said Nicholas Heymann. "The company has a tremendous amount of potential and it's just a question of executing it."

When it does emerge as an independent company -- technically, Westinghouse plans to spin off the industrial unit in about nine months -- analysts said the broadcast successor will possess strengths that set it apart from competitors.

"You have to give them credit on the network side," said Melissa Cook, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "Westinghouse has a lot more shows on the network schedule that it owns than the other networks." She cited "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" and "Walker, Texas Ranger" as two such titles.

As with other media companies, analysts on both the debt and equity side quickly turned to cash flow in their analysis. The issue is an especially important one in this case because of the media operation's debt load.
Early reviews were favorable, with Standard & Poor's among the first to weigh in, saying it was considering upgrading debt ratings for Westinghouse and its CBS subsidiary.

"Despite competitive challenges confronting broadcasters, Standard & Poor's views the combined businesses as having an above average business profile and the potential to generate significant discretionary cash flow," S&P said in a statement.
Heymann said the media company's plan is to nearly double earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to about $1.6 billion in 2000 from $875 million this year.

Some help will come from the fact that the media company will not be paying taxes for the next few years, as it works through the tax benefits of some $1.8 billion in net operating loss carryforwards inherited from its parent.
Also, Westinghouse's radio network, with the pending addition of Infinity, stands to be a powerhouse.
However, even amid expectations of stronger cash flows, analysts cautioned that many hurdles remain.

"The biggest challenge is to get the owned and operated stations turned around," Cook said. "If you look at the low margins in the station group, those could be a big driver of growth and the key to hitting their cash flow target."
Despite the positive reviews, Westinghouse shares fell one point to 19-5/8 on the session. Some of the sell-off may have stemmed from troublesome developments at the industrial company, Heymann said.

"One of the things that may have spooked people is a warranty provision (at the industrial company) of about $900 million," said Heymann. He also noted that Westinghouse revealed additional underfunded pension liabilities of $300 million, also to be allocated to the industrial arm.
"Maybe the fact that you have to put everything on the table gave people room for pause," he said.
A side benefit to unlocking media's growth potential is that the move may help Wall Street re-embrace a company whose languishing share price long ago disenchanted many investors.
"This is now a more focused company and you're better off owning a focused company," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.

Cripps said the fact that the industrial business offered little growth opportunity cast a pall, fairly or not, over the outlook for the entire company, adding that, "We, like many firms, were covering Westinghouse with an industrial analyst."
